solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Small and flipping serious bunkers are things to catch drivers

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the word for serious is read back to front

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
deep thoughts are serious ones
on a golf course a bunker is a sand trap

explanation.surface: A complaint about tiny, seriously annoying obstacles placed to catch out motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word qualifying 'serious', but it turns that word round. Bunkers are golf hazards, also called traps.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed traps are stretches of road watched by police radar or cameras to catch motorists breaking the limit.

clue.text: Reject a lot of rubbish about writer and philosopher

indicators.note: to reject is to throw back, so the shortened word for rubbish is turned back to front
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: trash is rubbish, especially in American use
re means about or concerning, as in business letters

explanation.surface: Someone telling us to discard most of the rubbish written about an author who was also a thinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reject' looks like the verb of the surface sentence, but it signals turning the shortened rubbish word round; the definition covers Sartre's double career.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre was a French novelist, playwright and existentialist thinker, so he fits both halves of the description.

clue.text: Plant that might be put in joint

blocks.note: en is French for in, as in a dish cooked en croute, put in a pastry case
a dive is a seedy bar or club, a disreputable joint

explanation.surface: A hint that some herb or weed might go into a joint of meat, or one that gets smoked.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests stuffing a joint of meat or rolling a cannabis joint; instead 'put in' borrows French en, and joint means a low-class bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Endive is a leafy salad vegetable related to chicory, a cultivated plant grown for its bitter leaves.

clue.text: Opener in dry season bats for ages

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters of the phrase it follows are scrambled
in places one element inside the rearranged letters of the rest

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
a key is what opens a lock

explanation.surface: A cricketing scene: the opening batsman in a dry spell bats on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' and 'bats' both point to cricket, but bats means mad and is the anagram signal. Donkey's years is a British idiom for a very long time.
explanation.definitionFit: Donkey's years is an informal British idiom meaning a very long time, as in 'I haven't seen him for donkey's years'.

clue.text: Royal has brilliant career

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN for Royal Navy
ace is slang for excellent or brilliant

explanation.surface: A member of the royal family is having a dazzling professional life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' looks like a noun for a working life, but it is the verb meaning to rush along headlong.
explanation.definitionFit: To career is to move swiftly and uncontrollably, the same as to race along.

clue.text: Sporting promoter occupies gym for the moment

indicators.note: sporting can mean playful or showing off, so the following word's letters frolic into a new order
what occupies something takes up position around it, so one set of letters encloses another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
PE, physical education, is school gym

explanation.surface: A sports promoter takes over a gym on a temporary basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting promoter' reads as a sports promoter, but sporting signals that the letters of promoter, with PE (physical education, school gym) placed among them, are rearranged together.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro tempore is Latin, usually shortened to pro tem, meaning temporarily or for the time being.

clue.text: Influential company take month off work

indicators.note: taking something off removes it, here the abbreviation of a calendar month

blocks.note: an octopus is a far-reaching organisation whose tentacles spread everywhere
OCT is the calendar abbreviation for October

explanation.surface: A powerful firm gives its staff a month away from work.
explanation.walkthrough: An octopus is a figurative name for a sprawling, powerful organisation; drop OCT from the front and OPUS is left.
explanation.definitionFit: An opus is an artistic work, especially a numbered musical composition.

clue.text: Rehearsal for short part of play, postponed?

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: pro is Latin for for, as in pros and cons
a play is divided into acts
a postponed plan is put on ice

explanation.surface: A question whether a rehearsal for a short scene of a play has been put off.
explanation.walkthrough: PRO loses its last letter; 'on ice' means postponed, so ICE stands for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice is a session spent rehearsing or training before the real performance.

clue.text: The usual flag

blocks.note: first meaning: the normal or customary thing
second meaning: a banner carried on a pole

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like ordering 'the usual' at a bar; the two parts are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is both a normal level or norm and a ceremonial banner, as in the royal standard.

clue.text: Whip up fruits

blocks.note: a jockey who is up is on horseback, riding
a crop is the harvested fruits of the land

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction to whisk up some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip up' looks like a kitchen phrase, but whip is the definition and 'up' means mounted on a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A riding crop is the short whip a horse rider carries.

clue.text: About to introduce museum's fizzy drink

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, about
the V and A is the Victoria and Albert Museum in London

explanation.surface: A museum is about to launch its own sparkling drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The V&A, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, is the usual crossword museum; CA comes first, introducing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cava is Spanish sparkling wine, made by the same method as champagne.

clue.text: Cage: "Why listen?", blasting this instrument

indicators.note: blasting suggests something blown apart, so the letters of the quoted words are scattered and reformed

blocks.note: a pen is an enclosure or cage for animals
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone named Cage, perhaps the composer John Cage, asks why anyone should listen to this instrument being blown loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: Cage looks like a name, suggesting the composer John Cage, but it is just an enclosure. 'This instrument' points to the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny whistle is a cheap six-holed metal flute, also called a tin whistle.

clue.text: Soldiers struggle with magazine?

blocks.note: the RE, Royal Engineers, are British army soldiers
to vie is to compete or struggle
W is the abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Troops are having trouble with a store of ammunition.
explanation.walkthrough: A magazine also holds ammunition, which suits the soldiers; the question mark flags that a review is only one kind of magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Review is a common title for a periodical, such as a literary review, so it can stand for a magazine.

clue.text: Nutty guys start to talk during act

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
what happens during something falls within its span, so these letters sit inside the word for act

blocks.note: a deed is an act
guys are men
the opening letter of talk

explanation.surface: Crazy blokes begin chatting in the middle of a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' could be a stage turn, but here it is a deed, something done, which splits open to hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Demented means mad or out of one's mind, and nutty is slang for crazy.

clue.text: Clear soldiers, with time, from the village

blocks.note: to settle a debt is to clear it
soldiers are men, as in officers and men
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An order to remove the troops, and time-keeping, from a village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' reads as an order to evacuate, but it means settle, as in paying off a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: A settlement is a place where people have made a home, such as a small village or community.

clue.text: You're supposed to go off in this carriage

definitions.text: You're supposed to go off in this carriage

blocks.note: surface reading: to depart, as a passenger setting off on a train
setter's reading: to drop off to sleep

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off' suggests a train departing; the real sense is falling asleep, which is what this railway carriage is designed for.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway car fitted with berths so that passengers can sleep through an overnight journey.

clue.text: Journalists in Spain, therefore getting black coffee

indicators.note: in places the word for journalists inside the word for therefore

blocks.note: E is Spain's international vehicle registration code
so means therefore
the press are journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Reporters in Spain, as a result, order strong coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: Spain is E here, its car registration code, not the ES of internet domains; the journalists go inside 'therefore', not inside Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: An espresso is a short, strong coffee served without milk, so it is drunk black.

clue.text: Make smaller type of bridge

blocks.note: first meaning: to shrink or tighten
second meaning: the standard form of the card game bridge

explanation.walkthrough: Bridge suggests a structure across a river; it is the card game, whose usual form has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to shrink, and contract bridge is the scoring form of the card game now played everywhere.

clue.text: After end of series rotten show travels — but not very far

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter
letters that travel move about from where they started, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: the final letter of series
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Following the finale of a TV series, a dreadful programme goes on tour, though not far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'travels' does that job, and 'After' puts the anagram after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A stone's throw is an idiom for a short distance, as far as a stone can be thrown.

clue.text: Repeat the usual claptrap

blocks.note: par is the normal or average level, as in 'up to par'
rot is nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone churning out the same old nonsense yet again.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests repeating tired nonsense, but 'Repeat' alone is the definition and the rest is the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to repeat words mechanically without understanding, as the talking bird does.

clue.text: It's good to wander in a punt

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to amble is to walk slowly, to wander

explanation.surface: Someone says it is pleasant to drift about in a flat river boat.
explanation.walkthrough: A punt suggests the flat boat poled along rivers at Oxford and Cambridge, but here it is British slang for a bet.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a punt is a bet, so taking a punt is taking a gamble.

clue.text: Being this 1 Down 'ad too many!

indicators.note: having had too many drinks leaves one reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: the answer to 1 Down, the French philosopher
had with its h dropped, as in casual speech

explanation.surface: A joke that the philosopher was blind drunk, having had one too many.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the drunken state is what jumbles the letters. Rat-arsed is vulgar British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has had too many drinks is intoxicated, which is what this coarse British slang term means.

clue.text: One villain in California is a chirpy type

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the abbreviation for the state

blocks.note: CA is the postal abbreviation for California
I is the Roman numeral for one
a cad is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A bad guy out in California turns out to be a cheerful sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chirpy' seems to mean cheerful, but it is literal: the insect chirps.
explanation.definitionFit: The cicada is an insect famous for the loud shrill chirping sound the males make.

clue.text: Superior adhesive's used up

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: gum is glue, and the 's adds the S

explanation.surface: A high-quality glue has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superior' looks like praise for the adhesive, but it is the definition, meaning self-satisfied.
explanation.definitionFit: Smug means self-satisfied and condescending, the attitude of someone feeling superior to others.

clue.text: Last in Oaks? You can have a punt on it but it's a fiddle!

indicators.note: the last in a word is its final letter

blocks.note: the final letter of Oaks

blocks.clueFragment: You can have a punt on it
blocks.note: the Cam is the river in Cambridge, famous for punting

explanation.surface: A betting tip on the Oaks horse race, with the warning that it is rigged.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oaks is an English horse race, so 'punt' suggests a bet, but here it means the flat-bottomed boat poled along the river Cam.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a swindle, and a fiddle is British slang for a dishonest dodge.

clue.text: Solitary carp, an aquatic creature

blocks.note: a hermit lives alone
to carp and to crab both mean to grumble

explanation.surface: A lone carp is described as a water creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carp' looks like the fish, which fits 'aquatic', but it is the verb meaning complain.
explanation.definitionFit: The hermit crab is a sea crustacean that lives in an empty shell borrowed from another animal.

clue.text: Extravagant oil, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: OTT, over the top, means excessive
the first letter of oil

explanation.surface: Mainly a lavish use of oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil' does double duty: it is the definition and also gives its own first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto, also called attar, is a fragrant essential oil distilled from rose petals.

clue.text: Evil test with beagle is something some folk find creepy

indicators.note: evil suggests something corrupted or warped, so the letters that follow are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: letters to rearrange
letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Animal testing on a beagle is something many people find sinister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creepy' seems to mean sinister, but it is the creepy-crawly sense: an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The stag beetle is a large insect with antler-like jaws, the kind of creepy-crawly that makes some people shudder.
